title: Man. Post. Cap. X tip — GAR.3: distinguish Christ’s act from fruit; Adam’s act from reatus
pass_a_gloss: Garissoles’ third: solve both sides by distinction. In Christ’s obedience separate the act from the fruit, and existence from imputation—the actual obedience no longer exists as act, yet endures to the age’s end by imputation and fruit (Rom 5:19). Likewise in Adam’s first sin separate the act from the guilt: the act passed in a moment and did not last until the law, but the reatus perseveres to the world’s end as it descends on each natural descendant (Rom 5:16).
pass_b_english: GAR. 3. But the objection will easily be solved on both sides if we use a distinction.
For in Christ’s obedience the act is to be distinguished from the fruit, and existence from imputation.

For although that actual obedience no longer is, as to act and existence, yet it endures, and will persevere to the end of the age, as to imputation and fruit, insofar as by his obedience many are constituted righteous (Rom. 5:19).

So in that first sin of Adam it is fair to distinguish the act from the guilt: that we may say the act indeed did not last until the law, since it passed in a moment, but that the guilt will persevere to the end of the world, seeing that it descends upon each of Adam’s natural posterity.
For guilt came from one upon all unto condemnation (Rom. 5:16).
source_text: GAR. 3. Sed objectio facile utrinque solvetur si distinctione utamur. Nam in obedientia quidem Christi distinguendus est actus a fructu, & existentia ab imputatione. Etsi enim obedientia illa actualis non est amplius ratione actus & existentiae, perdurat tamen, & perseverabit usque ad finem seculi ratione imputationis & fructus, quatenus eius obedientia iusti constituuntur multi. Rom. v. 19. Sic in Adami peccato illo primo distingui par est actum a reatu: ut dicamus, actum quidem non durasse usque ad legem, cum momento transierit, sed reatum perseveraturum usque ad mundi finem, quippe cum descendat in unumquemque naturalium Adae posterorum: Reatus enim ex uno venit in omnes in condemnationem, Rom. v. 16.
